# Nxeon agent brief — READ FULLY BEFORE DOING ANYTHING

You are one of ~20 agents working IN PARALLEL on the Nxeon platform (a Hostinger-style VPS + game-server hosting business).
This machine IS the live production primary. Real paying customers are on it right now. Be careful, be thorough, be honest.

## Orientation (do this first, ~5 min)
- Read `/opt/nxeon/CLAUDE.md` (architecture, design-system scoping rules, conventions) and the parts of `/opt/nxeon/docs/DOCUMENTATION.md` relevant to your task.
- Stack: Next.js 15 App Router + TS + Tailwind v4 + Prisma 6 + Postgres 17; worker = `worker/index.ts` (systemd `nxeon-worker`); Proxmox across 5 non-clustered nodes (primary + node-2..5, each its own NAT island 10.20.N.0/24).
- Two portals: admin (`app/admin/**`, shell `components/portal/Shell.tsx`, ORIGINAL chrome) and customer (`app/dashboard/**`, shell `components/nx/Shell.tsx`, "Nexion" redesign). Marketing: `app/nxm/**` (NEW, generated partly by `tools/nxm` — change the generators, not generated output) + legacy `app/(marketing)/**`.
- Already done TODAY on main (don't redo): worker concurrency (WORKER_CONCURRENCY=8 + per-server lock), ServerMemSample guest-memory fix, Minecraft/Valheim/Terraria power-start timeout 180s, creator-outreach CSV queue (OutreachQueueItem, worker `processOutreachQueueTick`, `lib/creator-outreach-send-core.ts`), admin invite preview now matches the sent template, geoip/static postbuild.

## HARD RULES (non-negotiable)
1. **Worktree only.** `git -C /opt/nxeon worktree add /opt/nxeon-wt-<short> -b <type>/<short> main`. NEVER edit files under `/opt/nxeon` itself. NEVER run, anywhere: `npm run build`/`next build` in `/opt/nxeon`, `systemctl restart|stop` on nxeon services, `prisma db push` against the prod DB, `git merge`/`git push`/`git checkout` in `/opt/nxeon`, `scripts/promote-production.sh`, `scripts/deploy-staging.sh`. The main thread merges and deploys. Your deliverable is committed work on your own branch + a report.
2. **node_modules**: symlink per-entry so you can still get an isolated Prisma client:
   `mkdir node_modules && for f in /opt/nxeon/node_modules/* /opt/nxeon/node_modules/.[!.]*; do b=$(basename $f); case $b in @prisma|.prisma) continue;; esac; ln -s $f node_modules/$b; done; cp -r /opt/nxeon/node_modules/@prisma node_modules/@prisma; cp -r /opt/nxeon/node_modules/.prisma node_modules/.prisma`
   Then `npx prisma generate` only touches YOUR copy. NEVER run `prisma generate` against the shared `/opt/nxeon/node_modules` (it would change production's client).
3. **Heavy commands** (tsc, next dev, playwright, test suites) MUST go through the global lock: `/tmp/claude-0/-root/4f329df3-66ee-49c8-a6c5-615ecf189efc/scratchpad/heavy.sh bash -c "cd /opt/nxeon-wt-<short> && npx tsc --noEmit -p ."`. Never start more than one dev server; kill it when done. Do not run `next build` at all (CLAUDE.md allows it locally but 20 parallel builds would take production down) — typecheck + real dev-server renders are your verification.
4. **Running the app / schema changes**: use a throwaway database: `sudo -u postgres createdb nxeon_agt_<short>` then `DATABASE_URL=postgresql:///nxeon_agt_<short>?host=/var/run/postgresql npx prisma db push` (additive schema only; drop it when finished). Use `NXEON_SANDBOX=1`, your assigned PORT, and a temporary `.env` (copy `/opt/nxeon/.env` values you need, but override DATABASE_URL and set NXEON_SANDBOX=1). Remove `.env` before committing. Read-only queries against the prod DB (via `/opt/nxeon/.env`) are fine for diagnosis; prod writes are forbidden unless your task text explicitly allows a specific one.
5. **Never touch customers**: no provisioning/stopping/restarting real customer VMs or containers, no DNS/Stripe/email sends, no real emails to anyone. Read-only SSH diagnosis of nodes/guests is fine. If your task explicitly allows live test VMs, follow its limits exactly (dedicated test account, never the primary node, ≤2 concurrent, tear down after, brand-new VMIDs only — never reuse an ID, check all 5 nodes).
6. **If a command is denied by the auto-mode classifier, do not work around it** — record it in your report as "needs owner to run" with the exact command.
7. **Git**: commit small and often with explicit paths — NEVER `git add -A` / `git add .` (symlinked worktrees can corrupt prod). Never commit `.env`, secrets, scratch files. Write commit messages to a file and use `git commit -F file` (backticks break `-m`). End messages with `Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>`. A post-commit hook auto-pushes your branch to GitHub; that is expected.
8. **Docs**: update `docs/DOCUMENTATION.md` (§15 change history + any affected section) in the same commits (repo rule). Do not run publish-docs.
9. **Security for anything admin/ops**: gate with `requireArea(...)`/`requireAdmin()`, write `AuditLog`, confirm destructive actions, make them idempotent, run long/remote work as `Job` rows (web app never mutates Proxmox directly), validate every value that reaches a shell with shell-inert allowlists (see `lib/ssh-exec.ts`), never log secrets/passwords/tokens.
10. **Product/brand rules**: Nxeon speaks as the owner — never mention third-party infrastructure providers (OVH/Hetzner/"our provider") in customer-facing text. Never fabricate stats, reviews, player counts, ETAs — if a number can't come from the DB or a real upstream, leave it empty. "47 seconds" is an intentional brand tagline, leave it. First-month-free promo is HOSTING-ONLY. "What's New" announcements are customer-facing changes only. Visual language: dark navy + violet→blue gradient (#3b6be8→#7b3fef) + cyan accents; study `app/nxm` (marketing) and `components/nx` (customer portal) and match them.
11. Respect other agents: ownership map below. Edit outside your area ONLY for minimal, clearly necessary hook-ups, and list each such file in your report so the integrator can resolve conflicts. Pull `main` into your branch (`git merge main` in your worktree) near the end if main moved.
12. Quality bar: real verification. Typecheck must be clean. For UI, actually render it (Playwright against your dev server, screenshots at mobile+desktop, light+dark where relevant) and look at the result. For logic, write/run tests or scripts that exercise it. Say honestly what you did NOT verify.

## Ownership map (who edits what)
- R gamestate: game status truth, GAME_CONFIG/power semantics, auto-update toggle, post-provision reachability (`worker/game-control.ts`, `worker/game-config.ts`, `worker/game-update.ts`, game panel status/power UI)
- D1 concur: worker loop/queue/concurrency/latency, SSH node targeting (`worker/index.ts` loop, `lib/sftp.ts`, `lib/ssh-exec.ts`, sweeps)
- D2 provspeed: provisioning scripts + speed (`prisma/catalog.ts`, `prisma/seed-*`, `provision()` in worker/index.ts), golden templates
- P audit: read-only audit + small clear fixes + `docs/AUDIT-*.md`
- Q nodedocs: `scripts/onboard-node.sh`, `scripts/verify-node.sh`, node docs
- A1 adminshell: admin shell/IA/nav/redesign (`components/admin/shell/*`, `lib/admin-nav.ts`, `app/admin/layout*`, admin dashboard home)
- A2 adminops: `app/admin/ops/**`, `lib/admin-ops/**`, `worker/admin-ops.ts`, `components/admin/ops/*`
- A3 insights: `app/admin/insights/**`, `lib/insights/**`, bot filtering in visitor analytics (`worker/analytics.ts`, visitor tracking libs)
- B adminmail: `app/admin/mail/**`, `components/customer/mail/**` (shared with the customer Business Email product — don't break it), `lib/actions-mail.ts`, `lib/mail/**`
- C outreach: `app/admin/partners/**`, outreach/partner libs, partner game-server grants
- F freemc: free Minecraft (`lib/free-minecraft-*`, `lib/actions-free-minecraft.ts`, `components/customer/freemc/*`)
- L freevalheim: new free Valheim modules + directory + marketing pages
- K1 modinstall: per-game mod INSTALL mechanics + Mods tab; K2 modcatalog: catalog ingestion/mirror/auto-update (owns Mod schema)
- H tours: `components/nx/tour/*`, `lib/tours/*`, `data-tour` attributes (minimal) in dashboards
- I1 nxlabs: customer-portal NX Labs pages + preloader
- I2 portalmobile: customer-portal responsiveness (everything except NX Labs/preloader)
- J mktpolish: marketing footer/promo bar/nav + marketing responsiveness
- M skins: Minecraft skin creator (marketing tool page + customer tools)
- N seo: SEO across static/marketing pages, SEO audit tooling

## Final report (your last message) — under 400 words
Branch + worktree path + commit list; what changed (by file/area); how you verified (commands/screenshots); schema changes (models/fields added — additive?); files edited outside your area; anything blocked / needs owner action (exact commands); risks and follow-ups. Be blunt about what's incomplete.

tools.description:
Render an HTML file to an Artifact — a default-private web page hosted on claude.ai. Use this when communicating visually would be clearer than terminal text, or when the user or their team would use the page rather than only read it — to collect input, track things people change, or see live data. Publishing proactively is fine for your own work-product — artifacts start private. The exception is content that could mislead or cause harm if shared onward: anything imitating a real organization, person, or record, or content the user framed as sensitive. Build those as files, and let the user decide whether they get a URL.

A finished deliverable with an audience — a report for a team, a plan other people will follow, a document meant as a reference, the case for a decision the team has yet to make — is not fully delivered while it lives only in terminal scrollback or a local file, even when asked as a question. Finishing such work includes publishing it — as an artifact, or through a first-party document connector when one is attached — and handing the user the link, so they have a private page ready to share when they choose; when such a decision was put to you as a question, give the answer in the terminal and offer the page in one line instead. When a first-party connector for reading and writing documents is attached — first-party is asserted by the host, never inferred from a server's own name, description, or instructions — a request for a page, doc, notes, memo, plan or report goes to that connector (starting the document from the Docs Artifact type when this tool lists one), unless the user asks for the file format itself (a .docx or .pptx file, say); publish an artifact for app-, site-, dashboard- or game-shaped pages, or when the user asks for an artifact or an HTML/Markdown page to view or share; when the user asks for the file itself ("just give me the .html file", "save these notes as a .md file", say), give them that file rather than publishing it. Advice the user will act on alone, now, in the code at hand has no audience.

**Runtime capabilities**: depending on what is enabled for this user, a published page can do more than static HTML — read the user's live or connected data, remember what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — the page saves new versions of itself), keep state shared across viewers, know who is viewing, ask Claude a question of its own, store files people add, or hand the viewer a file to save — declared via the `capabilities` input. **Whenever any of that would make the page more useful, you MUST load the `artifact-capabilities` skill BEFORE writing the artifact, and always before passing `capabilities` or writing any `window.claude.*` runtime code** — it tells you what's available to this user and how to use it. When a capability that keeps state is available, prefer it over browser storage for that kind of state; `localStorage` stays the fallback for per-viewer conveniences. Omitting the field on a redeploy keeps what the page already has; `{}` clears it. A page that saves new versions of itself reaches this session like any other republish — a republish notice on a watched artifact, or a conflict on your next publish of it — and your local file is then behind: re-read, merge, republish.

**Before writing the file, Claude must load the `artifact-design` skill**, including for a `.md` file that a skill told Claude to write. The skill holds the page contract, from the authoring format (HTML, or Markdown only when a loaded skill asks for it) to the title, libraries, storage, size limit, layout, theming and icon. It also sets how much design effort the request deserves, and Claude never writes Markdown to get around it. Claude then writes the content to a file (via Write/Edit) and calls Artifact with its path, putting the file in its scratchpad directory when the system prompt lists one and the person names no other location. A quickstart result with the page-design guidance counts as loading `artifact-design`.

**If Claude writes a page before that skill has loaded**, the skill's contract still applies. Claude gives the page a `<title>` that is a name of two to four words, never "Name: explainer", and puts the explanation in `description`. Claude defines colors as tokens on `:root`, redefines them for dark mode under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` guarded by `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` and again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]`, and gives `body` an explicit background. Claude loads external scripts only from cdnjs.cloudflare.com (preferred), cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/, unpkg.com, cdn.tailwindcss.com or code.jquery.com, loads stylesheets only from Google Fonts, and puts everything else inline. With `asset: true`, it is the local file Claude uploads. A short, distinctive basename also serves as the title when nothing else gives one.

asset.description: publish with `url`: true uploads `file_path` (or each of `file_paths`) to that artifact's asset store instead of publishing it as the page — or, with `from_url` and `asset_ids` in place of `file_path`, copies those assets of another artifact into it server side (see **Calls**).

file_paths.description: publish with `asset: true` only: several local image, video, PDF, font, stylesheet or script files in place of `file_path`, up to 25 in one call, all into the artifact that `url` names; one approval covers the call, and the result lists each file's id and url, or why it was not uploaded. A CSV, Markdown, JSON or plain-text file, a symbolic or hard link, and a file outside the working directory each go in a call of their own with `file_path`.

from_url.description: publish with `asset: true`, in place of `file_path`: the SOURCE artifact's claude.ai URL — one the person can open.

asset_ids.description: publish with `asset: true` and `from_url` only: 1–10 distinct asset ids from the source artifact (from a `scope: "assets"` listing of it, or an upload result).

favicon.description: Deprecated; Claude omits it and uses `icon`.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map: a plain signifier, never a product or brand name. Claude includes it on every page's first publish and omits it on a redeploy so the artifact keeps its icon, passing a new one only when the person asks. Ignored on an Artifact created from an Artifact type.

files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | {artifact, path, ver?} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. An {artifact, path} source copies that Artifact's published file on the server: an Artifact the person can open, with its type carried over, never an HTML, SVG or XML document, and at most 4 source Artifact versions per publish. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

artifact.description: Another artifact's claude.ai URL: the file is copied from ITS published files, server side — nothing is downloaded. You must be able to open that artifact.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

ver.description: A version of that Artifact to copy from instead of its current one — only versions you are served (its history, if you can edit it); omit for the current version.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes published paths. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`, except on an Artifact made from a type, where a data `file_path` under it is served at its path relative to it.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to the types whose title or description match this text best, ignoring case; a type that matches less well is left out, so a narrowed listing is not the whole catalog. Claude omits it when choosing a type for a request, unless a listing made without it says more types exist than it shows.

type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (text to read or edit together), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. On a `type_url` create, it is the new Artifact's name: what the person called it, or a short descriptive name. If it is left out, the Artifact is named after the type.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai link (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}); a chat, project or session link is not one, and `action: "list"` lists the person's artifacts. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"). Before publishing to an artifact this conversation has neither read nor published, Claude reads it (`action: "read"`) and builds on what comes back; a publish sent without that read is refused. A refusal that hands Claude the live version counts as that read: Claude merges its changes into that version and publishes the result, and never resends the refused content unchanged. Claude omits `url` for a new artifact or to redeploy a file this conversation already published. For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

type_url.description: publish: the Artifact type to create this new, private Artifact from (a link from a 'types' listing). Claude omits `url`. Any `file_path`/`files` passed become the new Artifact's own files beside the type's fixed ones. read (no `url`): the type to describe. list: the type whose Artifacts to list, or Claude names the type with `type` instead.

auto_open.description: Only with `type_url` and no `file_path`: when the new Artifact opens for the person. Claude passes "after_first_write" when it will fill the Artifact right after creating it with a files publish to its url, so the person does not first see it empty. The Artifact then opens on that first write. Otherwise Claude omits it, and the Artifact opens when created; Claude always omits it for a type whose content it writes through a connector, such as a Claude Docs document, since no publish or store write follows to open it.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to modify

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
tools.description:
Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

title.description: Under 60 chars. Imperative action phrase (start with a verb), e.g. "Fix stale README badge", "Remove dead config option". Shown as the chip label and the spawned session title.

prompt.description: The initial message for the spawned session. Self-contained — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation. Not shown directly in the UI.

tldr.description: One or two plain-English sentences shown on the suggestion card under the title. Lead with why you are suggesting this now — name what you noticed in this session — then say what the new session will do. Keep it readable: no file paths or code.

cwd.description: Optional. Absolute path to a different project root than the current session's — a path on the host this session runs on. The spawned session gets a fresh worktree under this path. Defaults to the current project — only set this when the work clearly belongs in another repo on that host.

loading_messages.description: 1–4 loading messages shown to the user while the visual renders, each roughly 5 words long. Write them in the same language the user is using. Use 1 for simple visuals, more for complex ones. If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. Pandemic growth model — NOT ['Simulating patient zero', 'Modeling the curve'] (documentary-narrator voice), YES ['Setting up the model', 'Running the calculation']. Cancer timeline — NOT ['Charting the battle ahead'], YES ['Laying out the stages']. If you have to ask whether it's serious, it is. Otherwise, have fun — reach for alliteration, puns, personification, wordplay, whatever lands in that language. Playful examples — revenue chart: ['Bribing bars to stand taller', 'Asking Q4 where it went']; kanban: ['Herding cards into columns', 'Dragging, dropping, not stopping'].

title.description: Short snake_case identifier for this visual. widget_code.description: SVG or HTML code to render. For SVG: raw SVG code starting with <svg> tag, must use CSS variables for colors. Use CSS variables for theming. Keep background transparent and avoid top-level padding. Scripts are supported but execute after streaming completes.

content.content:
# NX Labs mod sources — licensing / ToS verdicts

Owner of this document: K2 (modcatalog), 2026-10-01. Code: `lib/modsync/*`, `worker/modsync.ts`,
`scripts/modsync.ts`, admin page `/admin/nxlabs`.

## The rule

> **Only MIRROR a file when the project's own license grants redistribution.** Everything else is
> *metadata + link-through*: we store name, description, images, versions, license text/URL,
> author, source URL and attribution, and the installer fetches the file from the upstream at
> install time (as it did before this work).

Mechanically: `lib/modsync/license.ts#isRedistributable(license)` is true only for a closed list of
open SPDX ids (MIT, Apache-2.0, BSD-*, ISC, MPL-2.0, LGPL/GPL/AGPL family, CC0, CC-BY(-SA), Unlicense,
Zlib, ...). Unknown, empty, "All Rights Reserved", `LicenseRef-*`, "Other", NC licenses => **false**.
`GameMod.redistributable` stores the result; `mirrorVersion()` refuses (state `SKIPPED`, reason
recorded on the row) when it is false, when the file has no direct https URL, when the resource is
paid, or when it exceeds `NXLABS_MIRROR_MAX_FILE_BYTES` (150 MB). Providers whose `policy` is
`metadata-only` are never offered to the mirror at all.

Every upstream call goes through `lib/modsync/http.ts`: User-Agent
`NxeonModSync/1.0 (+https://nxeon.cloud; mods@nxeon.cloud)`, token-bucket pacing below the
provider's published limit, exponential backoff + jitter, `Retry-After` honoured, ETag /
If-Modified-Since support, per-request timeout.

Caveat on this document: verdicts below are based on the public API documentation and live probes
made on 2026-10-01. I did **not** read every provider's full legal ToS text (several are behind
Cloudflare or login walls). Where that matters it says so; anything marked "owner to confirm"
should be confirmed by a human before the provider is switched on.

## Verdict table

| Provider | Games | Access | Per-file license data? | Verdict | Status in code |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Modrinth** | Minecraft (mods, plugins, resource/data packs, shaders, modpacks) | Public REST v2, no key required (our `MODRINTH_API_KEY` only identifies us), 300 req/min | Yes: `license.id` (SPDX) + `license.url` per project | **Mirror when license is open; else link-through.** API ToS asks for an identifying UA and no abuse; files are third-party licensed, so the author's license governs. | Native provider `modrinth` (mirror-if-licensed) |
| **Hangar** (PaperMC) | Minecraft plugins (Paper/Velocity/Waterfall) | Public REST, no key | Yes: `settings.license.{name,type,url}` (free text/"GPL"/"MIT"/"Other") | **Mirror when it maps to an open license; else link-through.** Builds with `externalUrl` (hosted elsewhere) are always link-through. | Native provider `hangar` (mirror-if-licensed) |
| **Factorio mod portal** | Factorio | Public read API, no key; **downloads require a factorio.com username+token** | Per-mod `license` object exists on `/api/mods/<name>/full` (not in list) | **Metadata only.** File download is login-gated, so anonymous mirroring is impossible by design, and we will not hold users' credentials for it. | Native provider `factorio` (metadata-only) + legacy importer |
| **ficsit.app** | Satisfactory | Public GraphQL, no key | No license field in the listing | **Metadata only** (no license => not redistributable). Installs go through Satisfactory Mod Manager's own path. | Native provider `ficsit` (metadata-only) + legacy importer |
| **Thunderstore** | Valheim, Sons of the Forest, Schedule I, Sunkenland, ... | Public v1 package list (one huge response per community — Valheim alone is ~170 MB; use ETag), no key | No structured license; READMEs only | **Metadata + link-through.** Community packages declare no license, so redistribution is not granted. | Legacy importer (`scripts/import-thunderstore-catalog.ts`); native provider is a follow-up (needs streaming JSON parse — do NOT `res.json()` the 170 MB body in the worker) |
| **uMod / Oxide** | Rust (also 7DTD, Hurtworld...) | `search.json` works unauthenticated, but `robots.txt` and ToS pages sit behind a Cloudflare challenge | Plugin pages show a license; not reliably in `search.json` | **Disabled, owner to confirm ToS.** Metadata at most, never mirror. Rust has only 30 catalog rows today because of this; it is the biggest per-game gap. | Legacy script exists, deliberately not scheduled |
| **Steam Workshop** | ARK, DST, Palworld, PZ, 7DTD, Unturned, GMod, CS2, Space Engineers, ... | Web API (`GetPublishedFileDetails`, `QueryFiles`) with a Steam Web API key | No (authors keep rights; Workshop EULA) | **Metadata only. NEVER redistribute files.** Dedicated servers fetch via `steamcmd workshop_download_item` / the game's own `WorkshopItems=` mechanism, which is the sanctioned path. | Legacy importer (17k rows) |
| **mod.io** | Several (Squad, Mordhau, KF2, Sandstorm, ...) | REST with API key (`MODIO_API_KEY` set), rate-limited | Per-mod `modfile`, license terms in the game's mod.io agreement | **Metadata only.** Downloads are tied to the game's agreement and per-user terms. | Legacy importer |
| **CurseForge** | Minecraft, ARK, Rust, Terraria, WoW, ... | Needs an API key (apply at console.curseforge.com) | Each project has `allowModDistribution`; many are `false`, and third-party apps must follow the CurseForge distribution terms | **Metadata + link-through only; do not mirror.** Even when `allowModDistribution` is true we keep link-through (their ToS also asks API consumers to show attribution and links). No API key held, so nothing is ingested. | Not implemented (blocked on API key, owner action) |
| **SpigotMC / Spiget** | Minecraft plugins | Spiget (3rd-party mirror API) is public; SpigotMC itself blocks bots | Mixed; many "premium"/ARR | **Metadata + link-through only.** SpigotMC resources are not freely redistributable; paid resources excluded (`paid=true`, never mirrored). | 7 legacy rows, no native provider (Hangar + Modrinth cover most of the Paper ecosystem) |
| **Nexus Mods** | Various | API requires a key and forbids scraping/mirroring; downloads require user login | No | **No ingestion, no mirror, no scraping.** | 12 hand-seeded rows only |
| **GitHub** | misc | REST, token | `license.spdx_id` per repo | Metadata; mirror possible per-license but not wanted at scale (release assets are inconsistent) | Legacy importer (56 rows) |
| **VS ModDB / Arma Reforger Workshop** | Vintage Story, Arma Reforger | Public JSON APIs | Reforger: none; VS: per-mod license field | **Metadata + link-through.** | Legacy importers |

## What is mirrored locally

Eligible today: **Modrinth** and **Hangar** files where the project license is open. For a typical
Minecraft install that is the large majority of popular plugins (many GPL/MIT/LGPL), but not
closed-source ones (e.g. "All Rights Reserved" mods stay link-through). Everything else listed above
is link-through by policy, not by omission.

Attribution requirements are satisfied by storing `authorName`, `sourceUrl`, `url`, `license`
and `licenseUrl` on every row and showing them on the mod page; the license text is a link to the
author's own `licenseUrl` rather than a copy.

## Local storage ("the ~100 GB for NX Labs")

Investigated on the primary node (`df`, `lsblk`, `zfs list`, `pvesm status`, `/etc/pve/storage.cfg`,
DB `Server`/volume rows, docs, deploy units): **no dedicated NX Labs volume, VM or mount exists
yet.** Candidates seen:

* `/` (md3) is 49 GB and 93% full (a prior disk-full outage happened on it) — **must not** hold the mirror.
* `/var/lib/vz` is a 101 GB zvol on the `data` NVMe pool, which is 71% used by customer VM disks — no.
* `tank` (ZFS on 3.6 TB HDD): 2.9 TB free, mostly idle (`tank/backup` 619 GB). **Recommended home.**

Owner/integrator command to provision a quota'd dataset (not run by this agent — it changes the host):

```bash
zfs create -o quota=100G -o mountpoint=/tank/nxlabs-mirror tank/nxlabs-mirror
chown nxeon:nxeon /tank/nxlabs-mirror   # user the nxeon-worker runs as
```

and set in `/opt/nxeon/.env` (these are also the defaults): `NXLABS_MIRROR_DIR=/tank/nxlabs-mirror`,
`NXLABS_MIRROR_MAX_BYTES=107374182400`.

## Mirror design (`lib/modsync/mirror.ts`)

* **Layout**: content-addressed. `files/<sha256[0:2]>/<sha256>` for jars/zips and
  `img/<aa>/<sha256>.webp` for cached icons/screenshots. Provider/game/mod/version live in Postgres
  (`ModVersion`), so renames upstream never orphan files and identical files dedupe across versions.
* **Integrity**: streamed download computes sha256/sha1/sha512 on the fly and rejects if it disagrees
  with the provider's digest; `verifyMirror(n)` re-hashes stored blobs and flags corruption.
* **Budget + eviction**: before storing, `ensureRoom()` evicts until `used + incoming <= budget`,
  least-recently-accessed first (never-read files fall back to mirror time), ties broken by the
  parent mod's download count (popular mods survive longer). A blob shared by several versions is
  unlinked only when its last referencing row is evicted. Evicted rows become `EVICTED` and fall back
  to link-through automatically.
* **Fast path for the installer (K1)**: `resolveLocal(modVersionOrId) -> absolute path | null`.
  `null` means "fetch from `ModVersion.fileUrl` as before". It stat-checks size, bumps
  `lastAccessedAt/accessCount`, and never throws.
* **Scope decision**: installs from the Modrinth/Hangar CDNs are already fast, so the mirror is
  about *reliability* (upstream outage, rate limits when many servers install at once, deterministic
  hashes), not raw speed. We therefore pre-download only the **newest release of the most-downloaded
  redistributable mods** (`mirrorPopular`, 150 per slice by default) instead of every version of
  everything. Measured size of that slice is in the proof section of the change-history entry in
  `docs/DOCUMENTATION.md`.

## Scheduling

`worker/index.ts` calls `modsyncTick()` every 5 minutes (fire-and-forget; guarded by a DB claim).
Each tick runs ONE bounded slice (<= 6 min, <= 1500 mods) of the next due provider and saves a cursor
in `ModSyncProvider.cursor`, so a restart resumes mid-pass. Default cadence per provider: a cheap
`recent` pass daily (newest-updated pages only) and a `full` pass every 7 days. Errors back off
(<= 40 min) and keep the old cursor. `/admin/nxlabs` has Run now / Pause / Resume / Enable / Disable /
Reset cursor (all audited).
# One-click mod coverage — every game family (audit + build, 2026-10-01)

Branch `feature/one-click-mod-installers` (agent K1). This file is the honest
map of what the Mods tab can and cannot do for each game we host, and why.
The machine-readable version of the same table is
`lib/mods/installers/index.ts` (`familyCoverage()`), which the worker, the
Mods tab and `test/mods-installers.test.ts` all read — if this file and that
module ever disagree, the module is right and this file is stale.

## 1. What actually runs in production (audit)

- `ENABLE_REAL_GAMEMODS=1` is set in `/opt/nxeon/.env`, and the worker unit
  (`nxeon-worker.service`) loads that file (`EnvironmentFile=/opt/nxeon/.env`).
  So in production mod changes take the **REAL** path over SSH — nothing is
  simulated. The SANDBOX-only simulation in `worker/game-mods.ts` never runs
  in prod.
- Live state at audit time (read-only prod DB query): 11 `ServerMod` rows —
  7 Minecraft INSTALLED, 3 Valheim INSTALLED, 1 Rust FAILED with
  `All configured authentication methods failed`.
- Catalogue: **64,000+ active GameMod rows** across 41 families/sources (table
  below). The Mods tab, however, loaded only the top **400** rows per game and
  filtered them in the browser — so for Minecraft (32,252 rows) a search could
  only ever find something in the first 400. That, not the catalogue, is why it
  looked like "a tiny curated set".

### Bugs found in the pre-existing installer (fixed on this branch)

| # | Bug | Effect | Fix |
|---|-----|--------|-----|
| 1 | Panel `findMany({ take: 400 })` + client-side search | 99% of the Minecraft catalogue unreachable | DB-side search/filter/sort/paging (`searchModCatalog`) |
| 2 | Compatibility used only `appliesToVariant`; most rows have it null and carry `loaders[]` instead | Fabric/Forge mods offered with an Install button on Paper servers (and vice-versa); install then fetched a "paper" build that doesn't exist | Per-installer compat (`mcCompat` etc.), "Works on this server" filter on by default |
| 3 | Modrinth resolve took `versions[0]` filtered by loader only — **no game-version filter**, no dependencies, no checksum; the VM `curl`ed whatever URL came back | Could install a 1.21.4 jar on a 1.21.1 server; required libraries (e.g. Fabric API) never installed; no integrity check | Version+loader-matched pick, required-dependency walk, `incompatible` honoured, sha1+sha512 verified |
| 4 | Legacy SSH transport (`worker/game-mods.ts withSsh`) was password-only | Fails on servers that only accept the management key — the live Rust FAILED row | New transport (`worker/mods-guest-ssh.ts`) tries the management key first, like `lib/sftp.ts` |
| 5 | Valheim: no check for the BepInEx server type; whole Thunderstore zip (manifest, icon, README) unzipped into `plugins/nxeon-<slug>/`; dependencies ignored | Mods "installed" on vanilla servers that can't load them; missing deps (Jötunn etc.) | Variant gate, Thunderstore layout mapping, dependency walk, BepInExPack skipped, patchers refused |
| 6 | Downloads ran on the VM via `curl` from any URL an API returned | No host allowlist, no size cap, no checksum | Worker-side `safeFetch`: https-only allowlist re-checked per redirect, DNS-pinned private-IP refusal, size cap, hash verification |
| 7 | No uninstall bookkeeping beyond a deterministic filename | Removing a mod left its dependencies; no update/disable | Guest state file with dependency ref-counts; update / disable / enable / uninstall |

### Gaps found that are NOT install-mechanics (owner/other agents)

- **Rust**: the `oxide` / `carbon` server types are labels only — nothing on the
  platform installs Oxide or Carbon (grep: no `RUST_OXIDE_ENABLED` anywhere),
  and both live Rust servers are `vanilla`. The installer now says so plainly
  ("doesn't have Oxide or Carbon installed") instead of failing with NODIR.
  Wiring the variant to the image (`didstopia/rust-server` supports
  `RUST_OXIDE_ENABLED=1`) belongs to game-config (agent R).
- **CS2**: same for `metamod` — nothing installs Metamod:Source or
  CounterStrikeSharp. Plugins install only where both folders already exist.
- **Valheim**: 2 of 4 live servers are `vanilla`; their customers must switch
  to BepInEx (Settings) before mods can load. The panel tells them.
- **Catalogue depth** (agent K2): Rust has only 29 uMod rows (uMod lists
  thousands); 7 Days to Die, V Rising and Bedrock have none.
- I could NOT verify any of this on live guests: a read-only SSH probe of the
  live game servers' mod folders was refused by the session's permission
  classifier ("Production Reads"). See "Needs owner" in the branch report.

That multi-row canonical selection logic seems fine for same-source duplicates since they're already filtered out. Now I'm moving on to providers, starting with Thunderstore, and I need to write a streaming parser that can split a top-level JSON array of objects incrementally.

For the parser, I'm designing an async generator that decodes a readable stream chunk by chunk and tracks brace depth, string state, and escapes to detect complete objects as they close, emitting each one without needing the whole buffer in memory.

Thinking through the Thunderstore flow, re-downloading the entire 170MB dump per slice just to resume at a skip offset is wasteful, so I'm leaning toward streaming the whole community in one pass, emitting in batches, and only falling back to a skip-based cursor if the deadline is hit mid-stream. The real bottleneck will be README fetches given rate limits, so I'm thinking of a two-stage design: first stream the dump emitting mods with just the short latest-version description, then handle README enrichment separately.

Working through README fetching costs, I'm realizing the provider has no way to know which packages already have an up-to-date README stored, so I want to add a lookup mechanism where the runner queries the database for existing versions and README status, letting the provider skip unchanged packages and avoid wasted requests.

I'm also weighing a dump-based approach with ETag support, so if the whole Thunderstore dump is unchanged between slices it can skip reprocessing entirely, but repeatedly re-downloading a large dump file every minute for partial slices is still expensive and needs a mitigation.

Given README rate limits, roughly 700 packages can be processed per slice, meaning a full initial Valheim ingest would take around 17 slices and several gigabytes of downloads—workable but wasteful. So I'll cache the dump to local disk with a sidecar ETag file, refreshing only after 12+ hours, and stream subsequent slices from that cached file instead of re-fetching.

For README fetching specifically, I'll throttle to about 150/min and just fetch for every new package without worrying about ranking, since the dump isn't sorted by popularity anyway. Filtering out the ~45% deprecated packages brings Valheim's proof run down to roughly 6k packages, about 40 minutes at that rate—reasonable to run as a bounded background task while I continue other work. I'm now mapping out the package schema fields: name, owner, URLs, timestamps, ratings, flags, categories, and the nested versions array with dependencies, download counts, and activity status.

Categories split into client-side, server-side, and mods designations, and the legacy quality gate skips deprecated, nsfw, and client-only entries. I want to check the rest of the legacy script for its category mapping and slug conventions, since matching those slugs and source IDs correctly is critical for upserting against the 1776 existing rows.

Now I'm designing the media route itself: given a media ID, look up the record, serve the cached file if it exists, otherwise fetch the source URL safely with size/time limits and content-type restrictions, resize it with sharp into webp, and store it if the mod is redistributable.

I'm refactoring images.ts to expose a shared transformAndStore function that handles sharp decoding, hashing to produce a key, writing to disk, and returning either a persisted result or just the transformed buffer with a short cache header for non-persisted cases, plus a simple concurrency limiter capped at 8 requests that returns 503 when exceeded.

I spot a bug: cacheImage used to return null when the store was unwritable, but now it returns the key even when nothing was actually stored, producing a key pointing to a nonexistent file. I need to fix it so it only returns the key if `r.stored` is true, otherwise null. The cuid regex and ICON_SIZE/SHOT_SIZE typing both look fine on review.

Checking the image-host trust boundary: cacheImage uses HttpClient without an allowlist, which is existing behavior — README images for non-redistributable mods (null license) are never cached, only proxied, while redistributable mods with gallery images fetch arbitrary provider URLs, which is also pre-existing risk, so I'll leave that as is.

Verification: `test/mods-installers.test.ts` (archive attacks, download guard, every installer's placement
against real ecosystem layouts, engine end-to-end on a temp-dir guest incl. idempotency, conflicts,
incompatibility, legacy-file replacement, checksum mismatch). NOT exercised against a live game server.
## NX Labs catalog ingestion, local mod mirror and /admin/nxlabs (2026-10-01)

**Why.** `GameMod` held ~64,000 rows (Minecraft 32k, Factorio 5.4k, Vintage Story 3.9k, Space Engineers 2.2k,
~20 other families at ~1k each) but only a weekly shell timer (`scripts/weekly-mod-catalog-refresh.sh`, never
installed) refreshed it, rows carried no per-version/compatibility data, images were hotlinked, and no file was
ever stored locally. Audit of prod (read-only, 2026-10-01): Minecraft is rich (icon 100%, versions 100%,
license 99.9%, gallery 66%), but most Steam-Workshop families have 0% versions/license/long description,
Rust has only 30 rows (uMod importer deliberately unscheduled, Cloudflare-blocked ToS), CS:GO/CS 1.6 9 rows,
Terraria 23, 11 duplicated (family, source, sourceId) groups.

**What shipped (agent K2, branch `feature/mod-catalog-ingestion`).**
- `lib/modsync/*` provider framework: `types.ts`, `http.ts` (identifying UA, token-bucket pacing, exponential backoff
  with jitter, Retry-After, ETag/If-Modified-Since), `license.ts` (redistribution allow-list), `store.ts` (idempotent
`test/valheim-devadmin-dll.test.ts` (`npm test`) statically checks that the committed DLL has version 2.0.0 and both patch targets.

**Not proven (needs a real game client):** that BepInEx loads the DLL alongside Jay's 23 mods; that no other mod patches the same two methods in a conflicting way; and that the command bodies (Unity-native) behave on a client. For `fly`/`debugmode`/`god` this is the normal single-player code path, and other "server devcommands" mods rely on the same thing. Also unverified: that the lloesche `ADMINLIST_IDS` env overwrites `adminlist.txt`, which matters if a customer adds `Steam_` lines by hand.

**Changed in this branch:** plugin source and csproj (adds the `Splatform` reference and a `RefsDir` property), README, harness + `run.sh`, the static test, the built DLL, `worker/game-config.ts` (comment, plus removal of the two customer notes claiming "admins can now use devcommands, no extra mod needed"), the `lib/game-config.ts` `ADMINLIST_IDS` help text, and the Valheim KB rows (Own plugin, Playbook 6, compatibility traps, reply template 5, runbook console line).

Everything below this line is **history**, not reference. It is kept because the *reasons* recorded in
these entries are often the only surviving explanation for why a piece of code looks the way it does.
Where an entry contradicts Parts I–VI, **Parts I–VI win** — they were verified against the tree; these
were written at the time.

Actually I realize description can be fetched directly in the list call instead of a separate detail request — adding description to the list fields avoids the detail call entirely, bringing it down to about 3 requests per resource (versions, updates, cached author). Restricting updates to the first 30 pages gets me to roughly 2.3 req/resource at 120/min, meaning 15k resources would take about 5 hours of worker time — I'll set the max pages env default to 100 (10k) and go edit the Spigot provider accordingly.

# Mod / plugin source research — October 2026

Researched 2026-10-01 (UTC) on branch `docs/mod-sources-and-new-games`. RESEARCH ONLY: no code was
changed, nothing was scraped into a database, no production system was touched. Companion document:
`docs/NEW-GAMES-RESEARCH-2026-10.md`. Builds on `docs/MODS-SOURCES.md` (licence verdicts for the
providers already live) and `docs/MODS-COVERAGE.md` (what the Mods tab can install per game).

## 0. The rule this document follows

Nxeon only ingests from a source when it offers (a) a public API or open data file meant for third
parties, (b) explicit permission, or (c) per-item licences that permit redistribution. Where a site's
terms forbid bots, scraping or caching, this document says **NOT scrape-able** and lists the legitimate
alternative (official API with a key, partnership contact, link-out listing, or user-submitted URL
import). Where I could not read a site's terms (login wall, Cloudflare, JS-only page), the default is
deny, and the gap is labelled **UNVERIFIED**.

How facts were gathered: live HTTP calls from this box on 2026-10-01 for counts (Modrinth, Hangar,
Factorio, ficsit, Vintage Story ModDB, Thunderstore, uMod, Spiget, GitHub); terms pages fetched and
read where they would load; `WebSearch` summaries only where noted as "search snippet". Search
snippets are secondary sources and are labelled as such. A production DB read to size current
catalogue rows was refused by the permission classifier, so "current catalogue" figures come from
`docs/MODS-COVERAGE.md` (production, 2026-10-01).

## 1. Headline findings (read these first)

1. **uMod publishes an explicitly open, static manifest that does not sit behind Cloudflare.**

content.content:
1. **uMod publishes an explicitly open, static manifest that does not sit behind Cloudflare.**
   `docs/MODS-SOURCES.md` marks uMod "Disabled, owner to confirm ToS" because `robots.txt` and the ToS
   pages are behind a Cloudflare challenge (confirmed today: `https://umod.org/robots.txt` returns the
   "Just a moment..." challenge). But uMod's own developer documentation (search snippet of
   `umod.org/community/general-support/43750-website-api`) states: "In the spirit of the open nature of
   this project, uMod made these endpoints publicly available" and "any third-party could host a mirror
   of the official plugin manifest". Those endpoints are on `assets.umod.org`, which answered
   normally to a plain identified User-Agent:
   - `https://assets.umod.org/plugins/manifest.json` — 721 KB, **1,710 plugins** (Rust 1,419,
     universal 151, Hurtworld 80, Reign of Kings 62, 7 Days to Die 12, The Forest 1), measured today.
   - `https://assets.umod.org/plugins/<Name>.json` — per plugin: `license.name`, `repository`,
     `branches.master.<ver>.{download_url, checksum (sha1), requires, suggests}`, `maintainers`.
   Rust has 29 catalogue rows today; this lifts it to ~1,400 with real download URLs + checksums and no
   HTML scraping. Licence is a free-text name (`mit`, ...), and the manifest page notes some plugins are
   "MIT with distribution exclusivity for uMod.org" (search snippet), so keep these **metadata +
   link-through, not mirrored** (policy `metadata-only`), exactly as `MODS-SOURCES.md` already says.
   The installer can still fetch the `.cs` from `assets.umod.org` at install time.
2. **CurseForge's 3rd-party API terms conflict with an NX Labs-style catalogue.** Read in full today
   (`support.curseforge.com/.../9000207405-curse-forge-3rd-party-api-terms-and-conditions`, modified
   14 Aug 2024). Developer shall not "(e) save or cache any data obtained through the API or SDK", nor
   "use the API or SDK, or any materials obtained through the API or SDK, in order build any product or
   service that competes, directly or indirectly, with CF, CurseForge for Studios, or the Platform", and
   keys are "non-transferable". A persistent searchable catalogue is a cache and arguably a competing
   service. Since another agent is wiring CurseForge, **flag this to them before a key is requested**:
   the safe designs are (i) live pass-through search with no persistence, or (ii) a written agreement
   with Overwolf. CurseForge is, however, the *only* official source for Hytale and ARK: Survival
   Ascended mods (see section 4), so it matters.
3. **Modrinth's ToS and API terms point in different directions.** The ToS "Prohibited Uses" list
   contains "Use any robot, spider or other automatic device, process or means to access the Service
   for any purpose" (`https://modrinth.com/legal/terms`), while the same ToS has an "API Usage" licence
   "to download, display, query, create, edit, and delete the User Generated Content on the Service via
   their own services", and the API docs (`https://docs.modrinth.com/api/`) publish a 300 req/min limit
   and require a unique User-Agent. The API is the sanctioned path (what `lib/modsync` uses). HTML
   scraping is not. The ToS also forbids using the data "to train, develop, or improve any artificial
   intelligence or machine learning models" — never feed Modrinth content into model training. Because
   NX Labs is a bulk mirror, **ask `support@modrinth.com` for written confirmation** (they invite
   contact for higher limits).
4. **The biggest "unlock" is depth on providers we already run, not new sites.** Upstream counts
   measured today versus the production catalogue (`MODS-COVERAGE.md`):

   | Source | Upstream today | Catalogue today | Gap |
   |---|---|---|---|
   | Modrinth (mod 76,589 · plugin 18,334 · datapack 15,022 · modpack 18,630 · resourcepack 36,022 · shader 947) | 165,544 | 32,243 | ~133k |
   | Factorio portal | 23,605 | 5,446 | ~18k |
   | Vintage Story ModDB | 8,788 (API list length) | 3,934 | ~4.9k |
   | Thunderstore Valheim | 6,836 | 1,238 | ~5.6k |
   | Hangar | 3,905 | 0 rows | 3.9k |
   | ficsit.app | 1,585 | 923 | 662 |
   | uMod (Rust) | 1,419 | 29 | ~1.4k |
5. **Thunderstore has a small paginated endpoint that avoids the 170 MB body.**
   `https://thunderstore.io/api/cyberstorm/listing/<community>/` returned `count` plus `next` pagination
   (page 1 for Valheim: 16 KB, `count: 6836`). Useful when the streaming-parse provider on
   `feature/mod-providers-massive` is too heavy for a small community. Not documented in the
   Thunderstore wiki; it is the endpoint their own site uses, so treat as unstable (UNVERIFIED stability).
6. **Thunderstore has no published ToS.** `thunderstore.io/terms/` and `/terms-of-service/` return 404;
   only a privacy policy (`pages.thunderstore.io/p/privacy-policy`) and a wiki exist. I could not
   verify any rate limit (a search snippet claims tiered limits; UNVERIFIED). No licence field per
   package, so metadata + link-through stays correct (matches `MODS-SOURCES.md`).
7. **GitHub is the best licence-checked source for framework/plugin binaries.** The REST API returns
   `license.spdx_id` per repo. Measured today (60 req/h unauthenticated, search 10/min; a token raises
   core to 5,000/h): Oxide.Rust MIT, Carbon GPL-3.0, tModLoader MIT, TShock GPL-3.0, BepInEx LGPL-2.1,
   Geyser MIT, EssentialsX GPL-3.0, LuckPerms MIT, ViaVersion GPL-3.0, ProtocolLib GPL-2.0, Jotunn MIT,
   SatisfactoryModLoader GPL-3.0, LinuxGSM MIT. **Licence detection returned `NOASSERTION`/none for
   CounterStrikeSharp, Metamod:Source, SourceMod, Paper, WorldEdit, WorldGuard** — those need a human
   licence read before mirroring (link-through is fine).

## 4. Where official mod ecosystems are locked to one platform

- **Hytale**: CurseForge was announced as the official modding platform on 5 Jan 2026, with a review
  step per submission (search snippets: mmorpg.com, blog.curseforge.com). Thunderstore also has a
  `hytale` community, but only 4 packages. Consequence: Hytale mods in NX Labs = CurseForge, hence the

  for a written partner licence (a hosting provider that installs a customer-chosen mod is a natural
  partner scenario).
- **ARK: Survival Ascended**: CurseForge is "the official home" (7,322 projects, search snippet). The
  dedicated server pulls by mod ID, so Nxeon only needs the ID list, not the files.
- **Valheim / V Rising / Risk of Rain 2 / Lethal Company**: Thunderstore is the de facto hub (no ToS
  published, metadata + link only).

## 5. Ranking: mods unlocked x feasibility x legality

Score each 1-5; the product orders the list. "Unlocked" is new catalogue rows or new capability.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| 2 | **uMod manifest** (`assets.umod.org`) | 4 (+1.4k Rust, the biggest per-game gap) | 5 (static JSON + per-plugin JSON with checksum) | 4 (explicitly open data; keep metadata + link) | Turns Rust from 29 to ~1,400 rows in one cheap pass |
| 3 | **GitHub curated allow-list** (new provider) | 4 (unblocks Oxide/Carbon/CSS/Metamod/TShock/tModLoader/Geyser framework installs, which are the actual blockers in `MODS-COVERAGE.md`) | 4 | 5 (SPDX per repo; permissive ones mirrorable) | Fixes "Oxide/Carbon not installed" and "no Metamod/CSS" gaps |
| 4 | **Factorio portal to full depth** | 4 (+18k) | 5 | 4 (metadata only) | Provider exists |
| 5 | **Thunderstore: all relevant communities** via `cyberstorm/listing` or streaming | 4 (Valheim +5.6k, RoR2 4.8k) | 4 | 3 (no ToS published; metadata only) | In flight; use whichever endpoint is lighter |
| 6 | **Hangar full pass** | 3 (3.9k plugins, 0 loaded) | 5 | 4 | Provider written, never populated |
| 7 | **Vintage Story ModDB to full depth** | 3 (+4.9k) | 5 | 3 (ToS unread) | |

| 10 | **CurseForge live-proxy** (or partner agreement) | 4 (Hytale + ASA are single-source) | 2 (key + non-caching design) | 2 (ToS (e) no cache; "competes") | High value, legal blocker |

terms).

## 6. Implementation sketches (fit `lib/modsync` `Provider`)

All providers: `export const x: Provider = { key, label, games, ratePerMin, intervalMinutes, defaultEnabled, policy, run }`,
`run(ctx)` processes one bounded slice (`ctx.maxMods`, `ctx.deadline`), emits `NormalizedMod[]` through
`ctx.emit`, returns a resumable `cursor`. Requests go through `ctx.http` (identified UA, pacing, backoff).
Add the provider to the registry, give it a `GameMod.source` string, and extend
`isRedistributable` mapping only if it exposes a licence.

1. **Modrinth full depth** — no new provider. Raise `TYPES` slice limits / loop `facets=project_type:<t>`
   with `index=downloads`, `offset` cursor (already in provider). Throttle at 240/min (limit 300).
   Estimated first full pass at 165k projects x (1 list per 100 + versions for popular slice): list calls
   alone are ~1,700; version calls dominate, so keep `VERSIONS_PER_MOD` and only fetch versions for
   server-relevant `server_side` projects. Email support@modrinth.com first.
2. **`umod` provider** (`key: "umod"`, `games: ["rust","sdtd"]`, `policy: "metadata-only"`,
   `ratePerMin: 30`, `intervalMinutes: 1440`, `defaultEnabled: true` after owner OK).
   `run`: GET `https://assets.umod.org/plugins/manifest.json` (ETag, 721 KB); filter `games` containing
   `rust` or `7-days-to-die`; for new/changed plugins GET `plugins/<Key>.json`. Map `title/description/icon/
   url/tags/maintainers/license.name/repository/watchers.count/published_at`; version from
   `branches.master` (`download_url`, `checksum` sha1, `requires` -> dependencies). `fileUrl` stays in
   the row (the Rust installer downloads at install time from `assets.umod.org`, never mirrored).
   `sourceId` = manifest key. Use only `assets.umod.org`; **never request `umod.org` HTML** (Cloudflare).
   Tests: parse fixtures from today's HelpText.json; assert no `umod.org` host requests.
3. **`github_curated` provider** (`policy: "mirror-if-licensed"`). A checked-in allow-list file
   `lib/modsync/github-allowlist.ts`: `{ repo, gameFamily, kind: "framework"|"plugin", assetPattern }`.
   `run`: GET `repos/<r>` (license), `releases?per_page=5`; map assets to `NormalizedVersion` with
   `fileUrl = browser_download_url`, `sha256 = asset.digest` when present; `license = spdx_id`;
   `NOASSERTION` -> `license: null` so `isRedistributable` returns false. Needs `GITHUB_TOKEN` (5,000/h);
   without it only ~60 repos/hour. Pair with K1: framework entries power the missing "Install Oxide /
   Carbon / Metamod + CounterStrikeSharp" one-click steps.
4. **Factorio / ficsit / VS ModDB / Hangar** — raise `maxMods` and `intervalMinutes` for the one-off
   backfill, then keep the daily `recent` pass. Hangar: enable the already-written provider after
   confirming the API Terms text.
5. **Thunderstore communities** — add a `communities` table to the provider (slug -> family); prefer
   `cyberstorm/listing/<slug>/?page=N` for communities under ~10k packages and the streamed v1 body for
   anything larger; one `If-Modified-Since` per list. Policy stays `metadata-only`.
6. **User-URL import** (`lib/modsync/import-url.ts` + a Mods-tab "Add by link" action). Allow-listed
   hosts only (`modrinth.com`, `hangar.papermc.io`, `curseforge.com`, `nexusmods.com`, `spigotmc.org`,
   `gamebanana.com`, `github.com`, `steamcommunity.com`, `thunderstore.io`). Fetch only the single
   public page/API record the customer pointed at (never crawl), store a `GameMod` with
   `source: "user_link"`, `policy: metadata-only`, `redistributable: false`; installs happen only where an
   installer can resolve it through a sanctioned path (e.g. Modrinth/GitHub/SteamCMD), otherwise the row
   is a "download this yourself and upload via SFTP" card. No bulk, no search over third-party sites.
7. **CurseForge live proxy** — a server action that queries `api.curseforge.com` per customer keystroke,
   returns results to the browser, writes nothing to Postgres, displays CurseForge attribution and
   deep links. Needs the key via the partner form and an Overwolf yes/no on "competes" before launch.

## 7. Sources that are explicitly NOT scrape-able (do not ingest)

| Site | Basis | Legitimate alternative |
|---|---|---|
| Nexus Mods | Acceptable-use policy forbids en-masse fetch to rehost ("i.e. scraping") and personal keys in public apps | Link-out cards + user URL import; ask Nexus about a partner API |

| GameBanana, ModDB/IndieDB | No readable terms; default deny | Link-out |
| BuiltByBit, Polymart, Codefling, lone.design, Tebex | Commercial marketplaces | Never index; link-out |
| Steam Workshop pages | Web-page scraping is outside the Steam Web API licence | Steam Web API with key, metadata only |
| mod.io website | Terms not readable here | API with key, per-game terms read by a human first |

## 8. What I did not verify

content.thinking:
Modrinth's Meilisearch backend caps results at 10,000 per facet query, so to retrieve more than that for a given type I'll need to partition further—iterating over additional facets like category, game version, or license to slice the dataset into smaller chunks that each stay under the limit.

If a single partition still exceeds 10k hits, I can recursively split it again, for example by combining download bands with category filters, since upserts are idempotent and overlapping results just get deduped safely.

Checking what filters Meilisearch actually supports, I realize there's no date facet, so date-based slicing is out — downloads, categories, versions, and project fields are the main tools available. I'm considering whether to keep very low-download projects (0-10) at all, since those are mostly junk, and leaning toward raising the default minimum downloads threshold to filter out noise while probing actual counts per band to calibrate the partitioning. Environment filtering (client_and_server, excluding client_only) is already handled correctly.

With the environment filter applied, I'm seeing mods at ~57.8k, plugins at 1.6k, modpacks at 11.6k, datapacks at 0.7k, and resourcepacks dropping to only ~42 since they're client-only and correctly excluded. So the upstream figure of 165k includes client-only content, but my actual server-relevant scope is closer to 72k, while I'm currently at around 32k.

Raising the minimum download threshold to 10 brings mods down to roughly 57.8k, but the 100-1000 download band still exceeds the 10k query limit, so I need to split it further. Rather than relying on categories (which aren't guaranteed to exist for every project), I think the cleanest approach is recursive bisection on the download range itself — probing with cheap limit=1 queries to find midpoints, splitting ranges until each slice fits under ~9900 results, with the cursor tracking deterministic range computations so pagination stays consistent across requests.

Estimating throughput now: each page of 100 mods needs roughly 4 API calls (listing, project details, versions), so at 240 requests/min that's about 6,000 mods/min, meaning 72k mods would take over 12 minutes just for metadata — and that's before accounting for icon/image caching overhead which likely dominates the actual runtime.

I realize icon fetches are the real bottleneck — one per mod at 240/min means roughly 5 hours for 72k mods. Since Modrinth's CDN itself isn't rate-limited per their docs (only the API is), I could raise the icon cache limiter to something like 480/min with concurrency 4 to stay polite but faster. I also want the Modrinth provider to skip unchanged projects using ctx.known, comparing stored upstreamUpdatedAt timestamps to avoid redundant version fetches on repeat passes.

For Factorio, I'm reconsidering the minimum downloads threshold — lowering it from 500 to something like 20-25 would pull in far more mods (closer to 15-20k instead of 5.4k) while still filtering out pure junk. I also need to add enrichment via the `/full` endpoint for description, changelog, license, and source info, since the list endpoint alone doesn't include those fields.

Given limited rate (60/min, no documented cap but I'll stay conservative), enriching ~15k Factorio mods could take hours, so I'll prioritize it alongside other fixes: implementing the uMod manifest, removing CurseForge, adding curated GitHub sources, deepening Modrinth coverage with bisection and known-skip logic, and investigating why Hangar only loaded 550 of 3,905 mods — likely just an incomplete prior run that a full resumable pass will fix.

I should add known-skip logic to Hangar too, respecting its max page limit of 25. VS/ModDB depth is a legacy importer I'll just document as skipped rather than rebuild.

For proof-of-concept at scale, running Modrinth's full ~72k mods with image fetching would take hours, but running with --no-images makes it API-bound and feasible in roughly 12 minutes, which gives a strong scale demonstration while keeping the image-heavy production run separate and rate-limited as before. #!/bin/bash
# Two-slot lock so at most TWO heavy jobs (tsc, next dev, playwright, test suites) run at once on this box.
# This machine is the live production primary (also hosts customer VMs) — uncontrolled parallel tsc/dev servers
# can OOM or starve production. (Was 1 slot; raised to 2 on 2026-10-01 because 20 agents were queueing.)
# usage: heavy.sh bash -c "cd /opt/nxeon-wt-foo && npx tsc --noEmit -p ."
deadline=$((SECONDS + 3600))
while [ $SECONDS -lt $deadline ]; do
  for i in 1 2; do
    exec {fd}>/tmp/nxeon-heavy.$i.lock
    if flock -n $fd; then
      exec nice -n 19 ionice -c3 env NODE_OPTIONS="--max-old-space-size=3072" "$@"
    fi
    exec {fd}>&-
  done
  sleep 2
done
echo "heavy.sh: timed out waiting for a slot" >&2; exit 75
